Bugaboo architecture

AcceptedPhase 3 of 5·2026-10-04

How Bugaboo is built: the big decisions, the parts and how they work together, how it runs when sold or served, the technology underneath, and the checks that keep the code true to this design. Feature IDs (like SEC-04) refer to the feature list.

How to give feedbackUse this page's comment button. Mention the section number shown next to each heading (for example §7.2), or select text and comment on it. Tapping a section number copies it, ready to paste into your comment.

Goals and constraints

Quality goals

Ranked. When two goals conflict, the higher one wins, and the trade-off is recorded in a decision record (ADR).

RankGoalWhat it means for the architecture
1Security, secure by defaultOne authorization path for every way in (UI, API, search, MCP, assistant, exports, notifications). Deny by default. Hidden data never leaves the server, not even as a count or an error-message difference.
2UXPlain, fast, works for people less technical than average. Common actions feel under 100 ms; the server sends only what a screen shows.
3AI integrationThe assistant and outside AI apps (MCP) act as the person, with that person's permissions, through the same code as the UI. AI proposes; people decide.
4Software and design architectureSSOT, DRY and ODR are mandatory. Clear module boundaries, testable core, generated code instead of copied code.
5Feature completenessThe feature list, with no architectural dead ends for later features.
6Ease of installationOne binary, an embedded database, a setup wizard.

Across all of them: privacy by design (GDPR) and EU product law (CRA, AI Act, Data Act, NIS2) are constraints, not features. See compliance.md.

Constraints

Technology

  • Server: Rust, latest stable (1.97 at time of writing), edition 2024. unsafe is forbidden unless an ADR allows it.
  • Browser app: TypeScript 7 (the native compiler) and React 19.
  • Exact versions: see Tech stack. Versions are pinned through lockfiles and updated on purpose.

Platforms

  • Server: Windows 10/11 and Windows Server 2022+ (x64, ARM64); Linux (x64, ARM64, any distribution, static build); WSL 2 uses the Linux build.
  • Browsers: the last two versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari, on desktop and phone.

Data and scale

  • Databases: SQLite, built in, by default; PostgreSQL 16 or newer for larger installations.
  • Scale target for 1.0: about 500 people, 1 million issues and 200 people working at the same time on one installation, on a 4-core server with 8 GB of memory.
  • One organization per installation. Projects separate teams inside it.

Distribution

  • Bugaboo may be sold (the customer runs it) or served (we run it). Both must work from the same code (DIST-01; review: checked at every milestone review).
  • No telemetry and no outside requests unless an administrator configures them (mail, AI provider, single sign-on, update check).

Licenses of third-party parts

The license of Bugaboo itself is not decided. Every part we ship must therefore allow both proprietary and open-source distribution (DEP-LICENSES):

Allowed in the shipped binaryNot allowed
MIT, Apache-2.0 (also with LLVM exception), BSD-2/3-Clause, ISC, Zlib, Unicode-3.0, MIT-0, CC0, Unlicense, BSL-1.0, CDLA-Permissive-2.0 (data), OFL-1.1 (fonts), MPL-2.0 (file-level, unmodified)GPL, AGPL, LGPL (static linking), SSPL, BUSL, "non-commercial" licenses

The exact allow list lives in deny.toml (the single source) and is enforced by DEP-LICENSES (coding-standards §5).

People and process

  • Implementation is done by AI agents in milestones, guided by these documents. Everything an agent needs must be written down (review: checked at every milestone review), and every rule that can be checked by a machine is checked by a hook.

NeighborDirectionTrustNotes
People (browser)inUntrusted input, authenticated identityEverything they send is validated and checked by the policy engine.

Control planeinTrusted operator, no customer dataServed model only. Emergency data access needs the customer's approval (DIST-03).

Trust boundaries

  1. Browser ↔ server: the browser is never trusted. The UI is a normal API client (principle 3); the server re-checks everything.
  2. Server ↔ AI provider: prompts carry only permitted data; answers are treated like text from a stranger. They may propose changes, never make them.
  3. Issue and document content: written by people, so it is untrusted in every place it is shown or sent: sanitized for the browser, fenced for the assistant, escaped for e-mail.
  4. Operator ↔ customer data (served): our staff and the control plane sit outside the customer's data. Access is an exception with approval and a log entry.

Solution strategy

The few big decisions that shape everything else. Each links to its decision record.

#DecisionWhyADR
1A modular monolith in one binary, with a pure domain core and adapters around itEasiest to install, secure (one process, one boundary), fast; modules keep it maintainable0001
2Tokio + axum + rustls for the serverMature, fast, memory-safe TLS, no OpenSSL to install0002
3SQLite by default, PostgreSQL optional, through sqlx and one query builder; the database schema is defined once, in RustZero-setup install and a path to scale, without writing everything twice0003
4One policy engine; data leaves the domain only as Authorized<T>; searches get permission rules compiled into their SQLMakes bypassing authorization a compile error, not a code-review hope0004
5Our own search language, one Rust crate, also compiled to WebAssembly for the browserSimple and Advanced search share one parsed form; the editor behaves exactly like the server0005
6Own fields stored in a typed value tableFast filtering and sorting on both databases, permissions per field0006
7An append-only event log with an outbox is the single source for history, notifications, webhooks, the security log, search indexing and live updatesOne write, many consumers; nothing can change without leaving a trace0007
8API first: the OpenAPI description is generated from the Rust code, and the TypeScript client from thatAPI types exist once (ODR); the UI can't use what the API doesn't offer0008
9React 19 + Vite + TanStack Router/Query + React Aria Components in the browserType-safe URLs, one cache for server data, accessible building blocks0009
10Design tokens as the only source of style, turned into CSS variables; CSS ModulesFour themes and the theme editor from one source; customization can't inject code0010
11One Markdown renderer (Rust), used by the server and, via WebAssembly, by the editor previewWhat you preview is exactly what others see, sanitized the same way0011
12The same binary is sold and served; served means one isolated instance per customer plus a control planeNo second product to maintain; strong isolation; keeps "one organization per installation"0012
13AI through one provider interface and one tool registry, shared by the assistant and MCP; AI never decides about peopleSame rules for both ways in; AI Act high-risk uses designed out0013
14One check runner (cargo xtask) called by Git hooks, Claude Code hooks and CI; Biome and ast-grep for TypeScript and pattern rulesChecks are defined once and behave the same everywhere0014
15Personal-data marks in the data model drive export, removal, deletion rules and the record of processingGDPR can't be forgotten by a new feature0015
16Full-text search inside the database (SQLite FTS5, PostgreSQL text search)Permission rules apply in the same SQL query; no second index to secure0016
17Background jobs in the databaseNo message broker to install; works on both databases0017
18One settings registry defines every setting once: storage, defaults, permissions, API and the settings dialogs"Everything configurable in the UI" without hand-building hundreds of forms0018

What we deliberately don't do

  • No microservices, no message broker, no separate search server, no cache server. Each would add installation steps and attack surface for a scale we don't need.
  • No plugins that run third-party code inside the server. Integrations use the API, webhooks and MCP.
  • No server-side rendering framework. The server serves a static app and a JSON API; this keeps the security boundary simple and the CSP strict.

Dependency rules (checked by cargo xtask check only ARCH-DEPS)

  1. bb-core, bb-searchlang and bb-markdown do no I/O and depend on no other Bugaboo crate except bb-core (searchlang and markdown not even that; bb-core uses bb-macros for derives at compile time only), so they compile to WebAssembly.
  2. bb-app knows ports (traits) only. It never imports bb-store, bb-files, bb-ai or bb-notify. Tests run use cases against in-memory fakes.
  3. Only bb-policy can create Authorized<T>. Its constructor is private to the crate.
  4. Only bb-api and bb-mcp speak HTTP. Only bb-server wires adapters to ports.
  5. The browser app talks to the server only through @bugaboo/api-client.

The core modules

bb-core

Newtype IDs (IssueId, ProjectId, …, all UUIDv7 inside, readable keys like WEB-142 outside), field types and values, domain entities, domain events, and the error code catalogue (one Rust enum; becomes OpenAPI, the TypeScript union and message keys). Entities carry personal-data marks (ADR-0015).

bb-policy

  • Permission catalogue (one Rust enum with plain-language descriptions as message keys).
  • Evaluation: given an actor and a project, computes the effective permission set and the field mask (hidden / can see / can change per field, per issue type). Cached per request.
  • Visibility: project tree, restricted issues, documents.
  • Search predicates: turns the actor's visibility into query-builder expressions that bb-store adds to every query.
  • Authorized<T>: the only way data leaves the domain. It carries the field mask, so projections drop hidden fields automatically.

bb-searchlang

Lexer, parser, syntax tree, canonical printer, checker and suggestions. Knows nothing about databases or permissions: the caller passes a field catalogue (the fields this person may read), so a hidden field fails exactly like an unknown one. Simple search (filter buttons) edits the same syntax tree.

bb-app — use cases by feature

projects, issues, relations, fields, workflows, tags, releases, search, boards, timeline, calendar, relation_map, time (timers, time entries, working hours, rules), documents, attachments, notifications, assistant, privacy, settings, themes, people (users, groups, roles), admin.

Every use case has the same shape:

pub async fn change_status(
    ctx: &Ctx,               // actor, request id, clock, ports
    cmd: ChangeStatus,       // validated input
) -> Result<Authorized<IssueView>, AppError>
  1. Ask bb-policy whether the actor may do it.
  2. Load, change and validate inside one transaction.
  3. Append domain events (same transaction).
  4. Return the result through Authorized<T>.

bb-store

sqlx connection pools, migrations (defined once with the query builder, run on both databases), repositories implementing bb-app ports, the search compiler (syntax tree + permission predicates → SQL), full-text search adapters, the event log and outbox, and the job queue tables.

bb-api

axum router; extractors that turn a session cookie, access key or OAuth token into an actor; CSRF and origin checks; security headers and CSP; rate limits; ?fields= projections; cursor pagination; ETags; problem+json errors; OpenAPI generation; the embedded static app.

bb-ai and bb-mcp

One tool registry (search issues, get issue, create, change status, comment, log time, …). Each tool maps to a bb-app use case, so permissions and validation are identical. bb-mcp exposes the registry to outside AI apps; the assistant uses the same registry but returns proposals for writes instead of running them.

Browser app (web/app)

web/app/src/
├── routes/              TanStack Router file routes; URL search params are typed state
├── features/            issues, search, board, timeline, calendar, relation-map, documents,
│                        time, dashboards, notifications, assistant, settings, admin, setup
├── shared/              hooks, formatting (Intl), query keys
└── main.tsx
  • Server data lives only in the TanStack Query cache, fetched through the generated client, keyed by generated query keys.
  • Forms get their validation rules from the server's exported schema; the server still decides.
  • Components come from @bugaboo/ui, built on React Aria Components; styles use token variables only.
  • Heavy features (timeline, relation map, document editor, workflow editor, theme editor, WebAssembly) are split into separate chunks and loaded when first opened.

Runtime

How the parts work together in the most important situations.

Reading an issue

sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser
  participant A as bb-api
  participant U as bb-app
  participant P as bb-policy
  participant S as bb-store
  B->>A: GET /api/v1/issues/WEB-142?fields=title,status,priority
  A->>A: session → actor (or 404-style error)
  A->>U: get_issue(actor, WEB-142, fields)
  U->>P: may actor view WEB-142?
  P-->>U: yes + field mask
  U->>S: load issue (only requested ∩ visible fields)
  S-->>U: row
  U-->>A: Authorized<IssueView>
  A-->>B: 200 JSON + ETag (hidden fields never serialized)

If the actor may not see the issue, the answer is the same "not found" as for an issue that doesn't exist (SEC-MATRIX).

Searching

sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser (Simple or Advanced search)
  participant A as bb-api
  participant Q as bb-searchlang
  participant P as bb-policy
  participant S as bb-store
  B->>A: search text or syntax tree
  A->>P: field catalogue for actor (readable fields only)
  A->>Q: parse + check against catalogue
  Q-->>A: syntax tree, or "There is no field called …"
  A->>P: visibility predicates (projects, restricted issues)
  A->>S: compile tree + predicates → one SQL query
  S-->>A: page of rows + next cursor
  A-->>B: rows (only requested ∩ visible fields)
  • Sorting, grouping and totals are only allowed on readable fields.
  • Every query has a time limit, a page-size cap and a complexity limit.
  • The browser runs the same parser (WebAssembly) for instant feedback; the server's answer is the one that counts.

Changing something

sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser
  participant A as bb-api
  participant U as bb-app
  participant P as bb-policy
  participant S as bb-store
  participant O as Outbox consumers
  B->>A: POST change status (If-Match: version)
  A->>U: change_status(actor, cmd)
  U->>P: may actor make this status change? (who can do it, only if …)
  U->>S: BEGIN · check version · apply · "must be filled in" rules
  U->>S: append domain event (+ outbox row) · COMMIT
  U-->>A: Authorized<IssueView>
  A-->>B: 200 (or 409 "Ben changed this a moment ago")
  S-->>O: outbox → history, notifications, webhooks, security log, search index, live updates
  • Optimistic locking: every entity has a version. A stale version gives the plain-language conflict message.
  • "Then automatically …" actions run as part of the same use case, as the same actor.
  • Consumers filter by the receiver's permissions before sending anything (e-mail, webhook, live update).

The assistant proposes, the person decides

sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser
  participant U as bb-app assistant
  participant C as Context builder
  participant L as AI provider
  B->>U: "Summarize WEB-142"
  U->>C: collect context as the actor
  C->>C: drop hidden fields and fields excluded from AI · fence untrusted text
  U->>L: prompt + tool list (read tools run, write tools return proposals)
  L-->>U: answer + proposed change (priority → Critical)
  U-->>B: answer (labelled AI) + proposal card
  B->>U: Apply
  U->>U: normal change_status / update path as the actor, marked "via assistant"

Outside AI apps (MCP) use the same tools through bb-mcp. Their token is the actor's identity narrowed by its scopes; write tools act directly only if the person granted write scope.

Editing long text (edit locks, ADR-0019)

sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Ana's browser
  participant S as Server
  participant B as Ben's browser
  A->>S: first keystroke in Description → take lock
  S-->>A: lock token (60 s lease)
  loop every 15 s while editing
    A->>S: heartbeat (renews lease) + private draft
  end
  B->>S: open WEB-142
  S-->>B: "Ana is editing the description" (read-only for Ben)
  A->>S: save (text + lock token + base version)
  S-->>A: saved, new version → "Saved"
  S-->>S: lock released
  Note over A,S: If heartbeats stop (tab closed, network lost), the lease runs out and the lock frees itself.<br/>A save with an expired or taken-over token is refused; Ana's text stays as her draft with "Compare and save".
  • Short values use only the version check (no lock).
  • Confirmed saves: the browser shows changes at once as Saving…, then Saved when the server confirms, or a plain explanation (conflict, lock lost, offline) that keeps the person's text.
  • Watching open items: every 30 s and on focus, the browser asks for the current versions of what's on screen; a newer version by someone else shows "Ben changed this after you".

Working hours

  1. Start work day creates a work-day record for today (person, start time, time zone).
  2. Breaks and the end are added the same way, or typed in later.
  3. The working-time rules of the organization's preset are checked after every change. Broken rules become warnings stored with the day; nothing is blocked.
  4. Changing a day in the past requires a reason. The event log keeps the old value; the person is notified if someone else changed it.
  5. A daily job deletes work days older than the keep-and-delete rule allows.

Removing a person (GDPR)

  1. An admin chooses Remove a person. bb-app::privacy builds a plan from the personal-data marks: what will be deleted now, what will be anonymized, what must be kept by law and until when (DATA-MARKS; legal keep periods: review (compliance.md lists them)).
  2. The admin confirms. A background job runs the plan in steps; each step is idempotent and logged.
  3. The person's name becomes Former user K7Q2 everywhere (a tombstone record replaces the user). Records under a legal hold are deleted by the normal deletion schedule.

Live updates (built last)

The outbox feeds a small in-memory hub. Each open browser tab holds one Server-Sent Events connection and subscribes to what is on screen. Every event is checked against the subscriber's permissions, then sent as a small "this changed" note; the browser refetches only what it shows.

Deployment

The same binary runs in both models (DIST-01).

Sold: the customer runs it (self-hosted)

flowchart LR
  subgraph host["Customer's server — Windows, Linux or WSL"]
    bin["bugaboo<br/>(Windows service or systemd)"]
    subgraph data["Data folder"]
      db[("bugaboo.db<br/>SQLite")]
      fl[("files/")]
      key["keys/master.key"]
      bk[("backups/")]
      cfg["bugaboo.toml<br/>(start-up settings only)"]
    end
  end
  pg[("PostgreSQL<br/>(optional)")]
  s3[("S3-compatible storage<br/>(optional)")]
  users(["People"]) -- HTTPS --> bin
  bin --> data
  bin -.-> pg
  bin -.-> s3
  • Install: download, bugaboo setup (data folder, port, HTTPS), bugaboo service install, then the browser setup with the setup code.
  • Start-up settings (address, port, data folder, certificates, database URL) live in bugaboo.toml or environment variables. Everything else is in the database and changed in the UI.
  • HTTPS (SEC-10): built-in TLS (rustls with the ring provider) with a generated certificate, a provided certificate, or ACME (V1). Plain HTTP is allowed only on this computer (127.0.0.1, ::1) or behind explicitly named proxies. Enforced by: the start-up settings check (tests sec_10_… in crates/bb-server) and SEC-HEADERS for HSTS.
  • Master key: generated on first start, stored outside the database, readable only by the service account. It encrypts stored secrets and backups.
  • Upgrades: replace the binary; on start, Bugaboo makes a backup, then runs migrations. If a migration fails, it restores the backup and stops with a plain explanation of how to go back to the previous version.
  • Also offered: container image (non-root, read-only file system except the data volume), winget/MSI, .deb/.rpm.

Start-up settings (OPS-10)

Read when the server starts, strongest first: command line, environment variable, bugaboo.toml, built-in default. Each setting has the same name everywhere; its variable is BUGABOO_ plus the name in capitals. Wrong values stop the start with a plain sentence (messages config.*).

SettingMeaningDefault
addressIP address to listen on127.0.0.1
portPort to listen onnone; the start stops without one (ADR-0023)
data_dirThe data folderbugaboo-data next to the program
database_urlsqlite:… or postgres://…; empty means the built-in SQLite file in the data folderempty
tls_modeself-signed, files or offself-signed
tls_cert, tls_keyCertificate chain and private key (PEM), with tls_mode = "files"none
tls_namesExtra host names or addresses for the generated certificatenone
trusted_proxiesAddresses of proxies that add HTTPS; with tls_mode = "off" only they may connectnone
log_levelerror, warn, info or debuginfo
max_connectionsMost connections open at once1024
header_timeout_secondsTime allowed for a client to send the headers of a request30

tls_mode = "off" on an address that is not this computer is refused unless trusted_proxies is set. The settings file can be named with --config or BUGABOO_CONFIG; without a name bugaboo.toml next to the program is read if it exists. Defaults are relative to the program's folder, not the current folder (a Windows service starts in System32); relative paths inside the file are relative to the file. With tls_mode = "files" on Linux, a key file that group or others can read is reported as a warning. Enforced by: review (the tests ops_10_… and sec_10_… in crates/bb-server cover it; no catalogue check yet).

Data folder

bugaboo.db   the built-in database (made by the store)
files/       attachments
keys/        the master key and other secrets
backups/     backups
tls/         the generated certificate and its key

Folders that Bugaboo creates are readable by their owner only: mode 0700 on Linux, and on Windows an access list that grants only the account running Bugaboo. Key and certificate files are written with mode 0600 on Linux. keys/ and tls/ are checked on every start and made private again if someone loosened them (Windows: the access list is reset to the running account, found by its SID, not its name). Certificate and key are written as new files and renamed into place (key first, certificate second), and a key that does not belong to the certificate is replaced. A self-signed certificate is valid for one year and renewed when less than 30 days are left at start-up, or when tls_names changes. Enforced by: tests sec_16_… and sec_10_….

One file per system (OPS-01, DIST-01)

cargo xtask build builds the browser app and then the release program with the browser app inside (rust-embed); --target builds for another system. Windows x64 is built on the development PC. Static Linux programs (x86_64-unknown-linux-musl, aarch64-unknown-linux-musl) are built by cargo xtask ci on Linux machines, which the CI workflow runs once the repository is on GitHub. Windows ARM64 waits for the MSVC ARM64 tools (follow-up M1-F01). The program has no edition or model switch: differences between self-hosted and hosted come from the settings above only.

  b1 --> bdb & bfl
  cp -- "operator API<br/>(no data access)" --> a1 & b1
  • One isolated instance per customer: own process/container, own PostgreSQL database, own file bucket with its own encryption key, own web address. No database or file store is shared between customers (DIST-02).
  • Control plane is a separate service: it creates instances, rolls out updates, runs and checks backups, and watches health. It has an operator API on each instance that can do maintenance but cannot read customer data.
  • Emergency access (DIST-03): an operator requests access; the customer's administrator approves in their own Bugaboo; access is time-limited and every action appears in the customer's security log.
  • Data location: EU only; the sub-processor list and data-location statement come from the control plane's configuration (DIST-05).
  • Switching: a customer can export everything and import it into a self-hosted installation, and the other way round (DIST-06).

Releases

flowchart LR
  src["Tagged commit"] --> ci["CI: cargo xtask check all"]
  ci --> build["Build matrix<br/>windows-x64 · windows-arm64<br/>linux-x64-musl · linux-arm64-musl"]
  build --> sbom["SBOM (CycloneDX + SPDX)<br/>third-party notices"]
  sbom --> sign["Sign binaries, SBOM, checksums"]
  sign --> pub["Publish: release page,<br/>update feed, technical file"]
  • Every release has: binaries, checksums, signatures, SBOM, third-party notices, release notes, known issues, and its support period (COMP).
  • Security fixes can ship as patch releases on supported versions.
  • The served model receives the same signed release; the control plane verifies the signature before rollout.

Cross-cutting concepts

Security

Sign-in and sessions

  • Passwords: Argon2id (OWASP parameters: 19 MiB memory, 2 iterations, 1 lane), checked against a bundled list of breached passwords. A wrong password and an unknown e-mail get the same answer and the same timing.
  • Passkeys: WebAuthn (webauthn-rs), as a second step or on their own. Two-step codes: TOTP with backup codes (stored hashed).
  • Company sign-in: OIDC with PKCE; group claims map to Bugaboo groups.
  • Sessions: random 256-bit IDs, stored hashed; cookie __Host-bb_session (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax). New session ID after sign-in and after any permission change; idle and absolute timeouts; Where you're signed in lists and ends sessions.
  • CSRF: SameSite cookies plus an Origin check plus a per-session token header on every change request.
  • Access keys (scripts, apps): bb_ + prefix + secret; only a hash is stored; shown once; scoped, can expire, can only narrow the owner's permissions.
  • MCP: OAuth 2.1 authorization server inside Bugaboo (authorization code + PKCE, dynamic client registration with an admin allow list), short-lived access tokens, refresh token rotation, consent screen per app.

Browser protections

  • Content Security Policy: default-src 'self'; scripts and styles only from our own origin, no inline code, no eval; frame-ancestors 'none'; require-trusted-types-for 'script'; images from our origin and data: only (outside images only if an admin allows the host).
  • Other headers: HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, COOP/CORP, a tight Permissions-Policy, Referrer-Policy: same-origin.
  • One header layer wraps the whole router, so pages, files, API answers, errors and 404s carry the same set. Enforced by: SEC-HEADERS (the check compares the header table with the values the integration tests expect, exactly; the tests assert the full set on a page, an asset, an API error and a 404).
  • HSTS is sent only when browsers reach us over HTTPS (here, or at a trusted proxy), and never with includeSubDomains (Bugaboo does not own the other names of its host). Lifetime: one day with a certificate Bugaboo made itself, so a person who trusts that certificate on localhost does not pin every other local tool to HTTPS; one year with a provided certificate or behind a trusted proxy. Enforced by: SEC-HEADERS (no includeSubDomains) and the tests sec_11_hsts_….
  • Compression: Brotli or gzip for text, but never for JSON (API answers, problem+json): a compressed answer that mixes a secret with text an attacker chooses can leak the secret (BREACH). Enforced by: review (a person decides when another content type needs the same care), backed by the test sec_11_json_answers_are_not_compressed.
  • Slow and many clients: a client has 30 seconds (setting header_timeout_seconds) to send the headers of a request, which also ends idle keep-alive connections; HTTP/2 connections are pinged at the same interval. At most 1024 connections (setting max_connections) and 256 TLS handshakes run at once. Request-body timeouts come with the first endpoint that reads a body (M1-F06). Enforced by: the tests sec_10_…slowly… and sec_10_no_more_connections….
  • Client address: the address of the connection is used, with IPv4-mapped IPv6 (::ffff:a.b.c.d) always treated as IPv4. X-Forwarded-For is believed only from a listed trusted proxy, and supports exactly one trusted hop: the last entry of the last header line is what the proxy itself saw; earlier entries are what the client claimed and are ignored. Enforced by: the tests sec_10_forwarded_for_… and sec_10_mapped_….
  • User content is rendered by one Markdown renderer with an allow list (ADR-0011). Attachments are downloaded, never rendered inline unless they are images or PDFs converted to safe previews.

Secrets and keys

  • A master key (outside the database) encrypts a key per secret (envelope encryption, XChaCha20-Poly1305). Secrets: mail password, AI keys, OIDC client secrets, webhook signing keys.
  • Key rotation is a CLI command and an admin action; old keys decrypt, new keys encrypt.
  • Backups are encrypted with a backup key derived from the master key, or with a separate key the admin keeps.

Limits and abuse

  • Rate limits per IP and per account on sign-in, search, API and MCP; slow-down after failures, never a permanent lock that an attacker could trigger.
  • Request size limits; upload limits per project; search complexity limits.

Authorization model

flowchart LR
  actor["Actor<br/>person · bot · access key · AI app token"]
  groups["Groups"]
  roles["Roles<br/>(sets of permissions)"]
  assign["Role assignments<br/>on a project and everything below it"]
  fieldp["Field permissions<br/>hidden · can see · can change<br/>per role (per issue type)"]
  vis["Visibility groups<br/>restricted issues and documents"]
  scopes["Scopes<br/>(keys and AI apps only narrow)"]
  actor --> groups --> assign
  actor --> assign
  assign --> roles --> fieldp
  actor --> vis
  actor --> scopes

Evaluation, for an actor and a project:

  1. Collect role assignments on the project and all its parents; an explicit deny on a lower project wins over a grant from above.
  2. Union the permissions of those roles; intersect with the scopes of the access key or AI-app token, if any.
  3. Build the field mask: for each field, the highest level any role gives (hidden < can see < can change), per issue type.
  4. Visibility: an issue is visible if the actor may view issues in its project and (it isn't restricted or the actor is in one of its visibility groups).

People: every person shown anywhere is a PersonRef, resolved for the viewer into a name, a role label ("a Team member") or Someone, according to Who sees people (ADR-0022). Hidden people information can't be searched or filtered either.

Enforcement points:

  • Every use case asks bb-policy first. Every result passes through Authorized<T>, which applies the field mask during serialization.
  • Every search gets the visibility predicate compiled into its SQL; the field catalogue given to the parser contains only readable fields.
  • History, notifications, webhooks, exports, assistant context and live updates apply the receiver's mask.
  • Tests: a generated matrix (roles × permissions × fields × entry points) runs on every build.

Data model

erDiagram
  PROJECT ||--o{ PROJECT : "contains"
  PROJECT ||--o{ ISSUE : has
  ISSUE ||--o{ ISSUE : "sub-issue of"
  ISSUE ||--o{ RELATION : from
  ISSUE ||--o{ RELATION : to
  RELATION }o--|| RELATION_KIND : "is a"
  ISSUE ||--o{ FIELD_VALUE : has
  FIELD ||--o{ FIELD_VALUE : defines
  ISSUE ||--o{ COMMENT : has
  ISSUE ||--o{ TIME_ENTRY : "booked on"
  PERSON ||--o{ TIME_ENTRY : books
  PERSON ||--o{ WORK_DAY : records
  WORK_DAY ||--o{ BREAK : has
  PROJECT ||--o{ FOLDER : has
  FOLDER ||--o{ DOCUMENT : has
  DOCUMENT ||--o{ DOCUMENT_VERSION : has
  BLOB ||--o{ ATTACHMENT : "stored as"
  BLOB ||--o{ DOCUMENT_VERSION : "file content"
  EVENT }o--|| PERSON : "caused by"
  • IDs: UUIDv7 everywhere internally; readable issue IDs per project, counting (WEB-142) or random (WEB-K7Q2X), with redirects from old IDs (ADR-0021); short names for projects.
  • Own fields (ADR-0006): one field_value table with typed columns (text, number, date, reference) and indexes per type; used by issues, time entries, work days, documents, releases and projects.
  • Relations: one table for every kind, including timeline dependencies; sub-issues use a parent column, shown as part of on the map.
  • Files: content-addressed blobs (SHA-256), referenced by attachments and document versions; deleted when nothing references them and no keep rule applies.
  • Time: all timestamps in UTC; each work day stores the person's time zone so "day" means their day.
  • Versions: every changeable entity has a version number for optimistic locking.
  • Edit locks: edit_lock rows (what, who, session, token, expires at) for long text and admin editors; private drafts in edit_draft; both deleted when no longer needed (ADR-0019).
  • Deleted items move to the trash (soft delete with a deletion date), then are removed by the keep-and-delete job.

Events, history and the outbox (ADR-0007)

Every change appends a domain event in the same transaction: who (actor), how (UI, API, MCP, assistant), what (entity, field changes before → after), why (reason, when required). The outbox delivers events to consumers that run after commit:

ConsumerUses events to …
Historyshow the change log (filtered by the reader's field mask)
Notificationsnotify followers and mentioned people (filtered per recipient)
Webhookssend signed payloads (filtered by the bot account's permissions)
Security logappend hash-chained entries for security-relevant events
Full-text indexupdate search text (inside the same database)
Live updatestell open screens that something changed (built last)

Consumers are idempotent and resume from their last position after a restart.

Privacy engineering (ADR-0015)

  • Every stored field is marked in the entity definition: personal data or not, category (contact, employee time, content, technical), and the legal basis note. Unmarked fields fail the build.
  • The marks generate: Download my data, the Remove a person plan, keep-and-delete jobs, the record of processing, and the data-flow map.
  • Logs hold IDs, never names or e-mail addresses; IP addresses are kept 7 days by default.
  • Former users: a removed person becomes a tombstone (Former user K7Q2); references stay valid, personal data is gone.
  • Legal holds: working hours stay until their keep period ends, even after a person is removed.

Search language (ADR-0005)

Grammar sketch (final grammar is part of milestone work):

search     = [ expr ] [ "sort by" sort ("," sort)* ]
expr       = term ( ("and" | "or") term )*
term       = "not" term | "(" expr ")" | condition
condition  = field op value | field "contains" text | helper
op         = "is" | "is not" | "<" | ">" | "<=" | ">=" | "in" | "within"
helper     = "connected to" key [ "within" n "steps" ] | "under" key | "blocks" key | …
value      = word | quoted | number | date | "me" | "today" | "in last" n unit
  • The printer writes a canonical form; parse(print(tree)) == tree is a property test.
  • Simple search edits the same tree; anything without a picker becomes an editable text button.

Settings and configuration (ADR-0018)

  • Start-up settings (address, port, data folder, database URL, certificates): bugaboo.toml or environment variables, written by the setup wizard.
  • Everything else comes from one settings registry: each setting is defined once (key, type, default, levels — organization / project / person — who may change it, help text key). The registry drives storage, the API and the settings dialogs, so a new setting appears in the UI without hand-written forms.

User interface

  • Server data: only in the TanStack Query cache. URL: the search, the presentation and the open issue live in typed URL parameters, so every screen is shareable.
  • Lean requests: each screen asks for the fields its layout shows (?fields=); lists use cursor pagination and are virtualized.
  • Text: every user-facing string is a key in messages/en.json (ICU message format), typed via generated keys. The hooks reject literal text in components.
  • Styles: CSS Modules using token variables only; generated token CSS per theme; no inline styles (CSP).
  • Accessibility: React Aria Components for focus, keyboard and screen-reader behavior; axe checks in CI.

Errors

  • One ErrorCode enum in bb-core (for example issue.not_found, issue.version_conflict, search.unknown_field).
  • The API answers with application/problem+json: code, plain-language message key and parameters, request ID.
  • The TypeScript client gets the codes as a union type; the UI shows the message from the catalog.

Observability

  • Structured JSON logs (tracing, one object per line on standard error) with random request IDs. One line per request holds the request ID, method, route pattern, status, duration and the client network cut short (IPv4 /24, IPv6 /48); never the path as typed, the query, headers, bodies, names, e-mail addresses or free text. Enforced by: DATA-LOGS.
  • Health endpoints: /health/live answers while the process runs; /health/ready also checks the data folder (and the database once the store exists) and answers 503 when something is missing; both are sent with Cache-Control: no-store; optional Prometheus metrics, off by default and protected.
  • The admin Status page shows version, database, disk, jobs, backups and certificate expiry.

Performance

  • Per-request caches for permission evaluation; ETags for lists and issues; Brotli/zstd compression.
  • SQLite: WAL mode, one writer task with a queue, many readers. PostgreSQL: a pool sized to CPU count.
  • A dataset generator (cargo xtask dataset --issues 1000000) feeds benchmarks in CI; budgets from PERF-01…06 fail the build when exceeded.

AI (ADR-0013)

  • Providers: one trait; adapters for Anthropic, OpenAI-compatible endpoints (which cover local models) and a test fake.
  • Context builder: reads as the actor, drops hidden and AI-excluded fields, wraps people's text in clearly fenced "untrusted content" blocks.
  • Tool registry: shared with MCP. In the assistant, write tools return proposals; nothing changes without Apply.
  • Output: rendered by the Markdown renderer with remote images and auto-links disabled; marked Written with the assistant when saved.
  • Hard rules (AI Act): no tools that rank, evaluate or assign people; no access to working hours; no mood analysis. These tools don't exist, so they can't be called.
  • Limits: per-person and organization budgets; each call logged with metadata (who, tool, size, cost), not content, unless an admin enables content logging for troubleshooting.

Technical debt we accept on purpose

  • No real-time co-editing in 1.0. Instead: edit locks with heartbeats for long text, drafts that are never lost, and confirmed saves (ADR-0019).
  • Live updates come last; until then, screens refresh on focus and after own changes.
  • The served model's control plane starts minimal (scripts plus the operator API) and grows when there are customers.

Tech stack

Latest stable versions, checked against crates.io and npm on 2026-10-04. Lockfiles pin exact versions; updates are deliberate (Renovate-style pull requests, reviewed). Every direct dependency also needs an entry in docs/third-party/ (coding-standards §5).

Architecture checks

The architecture is only true if the code follows it. AI agents write most of the code, so every rule that a machine can check is checked, by many small checks rather than one big one (ADR-0020).

How it works

flowchart LR
  cat["tools/checks/catalog.toml<br/>every check, once"]
  xt["cargo xtask check …<br/>implements every entry"]
  edit["Claude Code hook<br/>after each file edit"]
  commit["lefthook<br/>commit · push"]
  ci["CI<br/>all · nightly · release"]
  cat --> xt
  edit --> xt
  commit --> xt
  ci --> xt
  • One catalogue, one runner. Each check has an ID (for example ARCH-AUTHZ-ONLY), a plain title, the rule it enforces, the tool, when it runs and which files trigger it. People, agents and CI all run the same code.
  • Small and fast. A check runs only when its files change. Edit-time checks take under 3 seconds per file and commit-time checks under 10 seconds, so nobody is tempted to skip them.
  • Explains itself. A failing check prints one sentence: what's wrong, which rule, and where it's written down.

Groups of checks

GroupGuards
FMTFormatting: rustfmt, oxfmt (TypeScript, JSON, CSS), taplo (TOML), rumdl (Markdown)
LINTLinting: clippy, oxlint with type-aware tsgolint (TypeScript 7), stylelint, tsc type check, typos, lychee, actionlint
TXT / STYPlain words and design: no literal UI text, message catalog complete, glossary "don't say" words, tokens only, theme contrast
ARCHThe structure in this document: allowed crate dependencies, pure crates, WebAssembly build, Authorized<T> only from the policy engine, only safe types leave the API, HTTP and SQL only at the edges, events for every change, versions and edit-lock tokens on change endpoints, lean list endpoints, permissions declared, settings via the registry, AI tools only from the registry, browser uses only the API client, module map matches the code, docs change with boundaries, no unsafe, both databases tested
SECSecrets, dangerous patterns, the permission matrix, security headers, known vulnerabilities
DATAPersonal-data marks, no personal data in logs, one schema source
DEP / DOCThird-party register, licenses, unused dependencies, SBOM, generated files up to date, decision records name their checks
PERF / TESTBundle and WebAssembly budgets, query counts, benchmarks, accessibility, search round trip, edit locks
METAThe checks themselves (next section)

The full list, generated from the catalogue, follows this chapter.

Checks that guard the checks

Adding a rule should be easy, and forgetting part of it impossible. The META checks make sure that:

  1. Catalogue and implementation match (META-CATALOG): no check without an entry, no entry without a check.
  2. Every check is tested (META-FIXTURES): each has a "bad" example that must fail and a "good" example that must pass, in tools/checks/fixtures/<ID>/.
  3. Nothing is unchecked (META-COVERAGE): every file type in the repository is covered by a formatter or linter. Adding the first .sql, .yaml or .py file fails until a check covers it. This is the hook that asks for new hooks. Generated files need no check of their own; the few other exceptions are listed with a reason in tools/checks/coverage-exemptions.toml.
  4. New modules are declared first (META-NEW-MODULE): a new crate, package or top-level folder needs a module-map entry and dependency rules.
  5. Every rule is traceable (META-RULE-TRACE): each "must" in the coding standards, decision records and these chapters names its check ID or says review with a reason.
  6. Callers agree (META-WIRING): lefthook, the Claude Code hooks and CI call only xtask, with the same lists.
  7. Suppressions are visible (META-SUPPRESS): every allow, oxlint-disable, ast-grep ignore or "not affected" vulnerability statement needs a reason and an issue ID, and the total can't grow unnoticed. The file types searched are listed in xtask/src/checks/meta_suppress.rs.
  8. Checks stay fast (META-SPEED).

Adding a rule

  1. Write the rule where it belongs (coding standards, a decision record, or a chapter here), with Enforced by: <ID>.
  2. Add the entry to tools/checks/catalog.toml.
  3. Implement it in xtask/src/checks/.
  4. Add the bad and good examples.

The META checks fail until all four steps are done.

Sample organization

A realistic, fully fictional organization used for development, end-to-end tests, demos and the optional "try it out" mode (OPS-12). Generated by cargo xtask dataset sample, deterministic from a seed (default 42), in under a minute, into SQLite or PostgreSQL.

People (50) and groups

  • 2 Administrators, 4 Project leads, 30 Team members, 8 Contributors, 4 Viewers, 2 Guests, plus 1 bot account.
  • Groups: Backend, Frontend, Mobile, QA, Support, Docs, Management, External.
  • Generated names from a mixed international name list; e-mail addresses under the reserved domain bugaboo.example, so nothing can ever reach a real inbox.
  • Each person has a time zone, some have passkeys, two-step sign-in or access keys. Two people are already removed (Former user labels) to test GDPR flows.

Projects (4, two with sub-projects) — about 10,000 issues

ProjectShort nameIDsSub-projectsIssues
Mobile appAPPrandomiOS (IOS), Android (AND)≈ 4,800
WebsiteWEBcountingShop (SHOP), Blog (BLOG)≈ 3,000
OperationsOPSrandom—≈ 1,800, including restricted security issues
HandbookDOCcounting—≈ 400, mostly documents and tasks

What's inside

  • Issues over the last 18 months (dates are shifted at generation time, so the data always looks current): Bug 45 %, Task 30 %, Feature 20 %, Goal 5 %; realistic status ages, priorities and labels; own fields (Severity, Platforms, Customer); about 2 % restricted issues.
  • Sub-issues under goals, and about 3,000 relations of every kind, including chains deeper than four steps and one deliberate blocks circle (to test the warning).
  • Releases: three per project, one in the past, one current, one planned.
  • Comments: about 30,000, with mentions; some edited.
  • Files and documents: about 500 small generated attachments (images, PDFs), 60 pages and 20 files with several versions each.
  • Time: about 20,000 time entries with activities and cost centers, six months of working hours for every employee (including some broken working-time rules), and a few running timers.
  • Configuration: workflows for each issue type, field permissions (for example Cost center hidden from Contributors), Who sees people set for Guests, fields excluded from AI, saved searches, dashboards, two custom themes.
  • States worth testing: an edit lock held by someone, a pending conflict, a closed month, a person with a removal in progress.

Large dataset

cargo xtask dataset large --issues 1000000 builds the same shape at the PERF scale (500 people, 500 projects) for benchmarks.

Ten people at the same time

Concurrency is tested with 10 simulated people from the sample organization, each in their own browser context (Playwright) or API client (cargo xtask load --people 10):

ScenarioWhat must hold
Three people try to edit the same descriptionOne gets the lock; the others see "… is editing"; Edit anyway moves the lock and keeps the first person's draft
Two people change the status of the same issue within a secondOne wins; the other sees the conflict message; nothing is half-saved
A lock holder's network dropsThe lock frees itself within a minute; their text is kept as a draft and offered with Compare and save
Everyone drags cards on the same boardFinal board matches the event log; every person's screen shows the final state after refresh
Timers and working hours start and stop at the same timeNo double entries; working-time rules evaluated once per change
Searches while others change dataResults respect permissions at every moment; no errors; latency within budget

Enforced by: TEST-CONCURRENT, TEST-EDIT-LOCKS.

Each scenario runs against both SQLite and PostgreSQL. The short version (2 minutes) runs in CI; the long version (30 minutes, mixed workload) runs nightly and checks invariants afterwards: every change has an event, no lock outlives its lease, no text is lost.

Local ports (ADR-0023)

Your machine runs other Vite projects, so Bugaboo never uses default ports. All ports live in tools/dev/ports.json (single source); Vite, Playwright, the server and xtask read them from there, and every tool uses strictPort, so a busy port fails with a clear message instead of silently moving.

PortUsed by
47200Bugaboo server in development (API + embedded app)
47201Vite dev server (hot reload)
47202Vite preview of a production build
47203Server instance for end-to-end tests (fresh sample database)
47204Vitest UI
47210–47229Parallel Playwright workers, one server and database each
47230Load-test server
47240Throwaway PostgreSQL for tests (cargo xtask db start)

The installed product asks for its port in the setup wizard (suggesting 8443 and checking that it's free); these development ports never appear in a customer installation.

Part of the security and data-flow documentation (COMP-07) for the CRA technical file and for customers' own risk assessments. It covers what is built so far and grows with every milestone: each milestone review checks that new entry points appear here.

The method is STRIDE per trust boundary (boundaries from Context). Every threat names the mitigation and what proves it: a check from the catalogue (tools/checks/catalog.toml), a test, or review when a person decides.
